new.why: Shared inference fleets now expose priority, fairness and cache behavior as explicit production policies rather than hidden scheduler details.
new.summary: Priority-aware inference operations coordinate queueing, cache use and service isolation so shared model fleets honor differentiated workload objectives.
new.why_now: llm-d v1.0 on October 20 added multi-tenant fairness, priority-aware scheduling and zero-downtime operations with a reported deployment cache improvement.
new.practical_value: Platform teams can replay mixed-priority traffic and measure latency, starvation, cache hits and rollout disruption before enabling production policies.

novelty.reason: The release combines explicit workload priority, fairness and cache-aware routing within one operational inference framework.

evidence.reason: The October 20 release documents mechanisms and one cache result, while detailed independent reproduction remains unavailable.

independence.reason: The evidence comes from project maintainers and participating vendors, without an independent comparative production study.

momentum.reason: One release observation provides no repeated comparable service metric at distinct valid observation times.

relevance.reason: Inference operators can directly test latency, starvation, cache effectiveness and rollout continuity under mixed-priority traffic.

durability.reason: Queue fairness, cache placement and safe rollouts remain durable concerns across models, accelerators and serving stacks.

momentum.reason: No two comparable dated numerical observations establish momentum for this operational approach.

new.why: A small coordinator can preserve specialist context and tool boundaries while making routing and handoffs inspectable.
new.summary: Thin orchestration boundaries keep central agents focused on routing and typed handoffs while specialists retain narrow context and tools.
new.why_now: Meta’s October 19 engineering report describes a 1,300-line orchestrator serving more than 20 workflows through 14 isolated specialists.
new.practical_value: Engineering teams can compare one broad agent with explicit routing, typed handoffs and revision-rate measurements on representative internal tasks.

novelty.reason: The architecture sharply limits the orchestrator to deterministic routing and typed coordination instead of generalized execution.

evidence.reason: Meta supplies architecture details, workflow counts and internal delivery observations, but not a reproducible external benchmark.

independence.reason: All measured results originate from Meta’s internal environment and lack independent replication across another organization.

momentum.reason: Reported outcomes do not form two comparable observations under one stable measure at distinct timestamps.

relevance.reason: Teams facing context collisions can directly test route clarity, handoff completeness, revisions and specialist tool boundaries.

durability.reason: Separation of coordination and execution should persist, although optimal specialist granularity will vary by workflow.

momentum.reason: A single internal case study cannot establish numerical momentum over time.

updated.why: Plaud extends reusable skills into a noncoding meeting workspace with reviewed drafts, automatic invocation and explicit limits.
updated.what_changed: The October 20 Plaud procedure adds five noncoding creation paths, pre-save review, Work-mode credit costs and a 100-skill workspace limit.
updated.summary: Reusable agent skills package repeatable instructions that assistants can discover, invoke and apply to bounded work without restating every step.
updated.why_now: Plaud’s October 20 documentation provides a new noncoding implementation with draft review, automatic invocation and concrete operating limits.
updated.practical_value: Knowledge workers can fixture-test one meeting procedure, verify evidence links and costs, then approve the reusable instruction set before distribution.

novelty.reason: Plaud brings saved agent procedures into recorded-work workflows with several creation paths and automatic invocation.

evidence.reason: The official procedure specifies creation, review, invocation, editing, cost and workspace-limit behavior in operational detail.

independence.reason: Plaud independently implements reusable skills beyond coding clients, although the reviewed behavior remains publisher-documented.

momentum.reason: Different skill implementations publish features rather than one comparable outcome metric observed at distinct times.

relevance.reason: Meeting-heavy teams can immediately test a bounded decision-brief procedure against transcripts and human review criteria.

durability.reason: Versioned reusable instructions and explicit approval remain useful even as assistants, interfaces and billing models change.

momentum.reason: No stable repeated numerical outcome measure supports a momentum score for reusable skills.

carried_forward.why: No material new independent evidence changed the October 19 GRAFT assessment, so its prior reviewed rubric is carried.

carried_forward.why_now: No newer independent replication changed the October 19 GRAFT evidence, so the topic remains active without a material update.
carried_forward.practical_value: Researchers can continue bounded replications with held-out hacks, baseline mitigations and explicit task-performance checks before larger-model trials.

novelty.reason: GRAFT changes monitor use from reward shaping to gradient routing and removable parameter localization.

evidence.reason: The October 19 article provides code, a paper, controlled comparisons and explicit quantitative results across several small environments.

independence.reason: Authors span MATS, Stanford, FAR AI and Anthropic, but the reviewed results remain one collaborating research effort.

momentum.reason: No comparable repeated observation across dated production-scale deployments establishes a defensible momentum direction.

relevance.reason: Training teams can directly test whether adapter ablation reduces held-out hacks without erasing target-task gains.

durability.reason: The gradient-routing idea may endure, although anchor-environment requirements and larger-scale behavior remain unresolved.

momentum.reason: One research release lacks two comparable dated observations under a stable metric.

carried_forward.why: No material new recovery evidence displaced the October 14 guide, so its prior reviewed rubric is carried.
carried_forward.summary: Provider-aware failover routes repeatable inference work across qualified models while stopping ambiguous or stateful replays for reconciliation.
carried_forward.why_now: No newer end-to-end recovery guide displaced the October 14 policy, so the topic remains active without a material evidence change.
carried_forward.practical_value: Teams can keep testing one read-only inference step with central retry budgets, degraded paths and explicit replay-stop rules.

novelty.reason: The guide moves multi-provider resilience from generic routing into explicit per-operation replay and recovery decisions.

evidence.reason: OpenAI provides failure classes, implementation constraints, test cases and operational measures, though no independent outage study.

independence.reason: The guidance is authored by one model provider and lacks independent comparative validation across production gateways.

momentum.reason: This first policy observation offers no repeated comparable outcome measure for adoption, recovery time or errors.

relevance.reason: Platform and application teams can directly map retryability, deadlines, route approval and duplicate-action protection.

durability.reason: Safe retries, bounded failover and explicit recovery ownership remain necessary across providers and model generations.

momentum.reason: No two comparable dated numerical observations establish momentum for this policy.

dropped.reason: The topic moves to history because no independent workload evaluation has followed the October 14 beta release.
dropped.summary: SQL-native predictive workflows place maintained forecasting and classification models inside queries, dashboards and plain-language analytics tools.
dropped.why_now: No independent workload evaluation appeared after the October 14 beta, so the release signal is archived rather than carried.
dropped.practical_value: Retain the backtest checklist, but avoid treating vendor examples as evidence that built-in functions improve production decisions.

novelty.reason: The release packages familiar predictive methods into consistent SQL, dashboard and conversational interfaces for non-specialists.

evidence.reason: Databricks documents functions, examples and a named forecasting benchmark, while detailed reproducibility remains limited.

independence.reason: Benchmark and product evidence originate from Databricks, with no independent workload replication reviewed for this release.

momentum.reason: The beta launch supplies no two comparable dated adoption or outcome observations under one stable measure.

relevance.reason: Knowledge teams can evaluate forecasts, anomalies and drivers directly inside governed data workflows they already use.
